title: Merge vs rebase
description: Learn about Merge vs rebase. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Merge vs rebase is one of the most debated topics in Git. Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they produce different histories, conflict behaviors, and team workflows.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers merge commits, fast-forward merges, rebasing, visual comparisons, team conventions, and hybrid workflows.

A merge combines the histories of two branches. Git creates a merge commit with two parents, representing the point where the branches came together. If the branches can be connected linearly, Git performs a fast-forward merge.

data.title: Merge Example
data.code:
git checkout main
git merge feature/user-profile

# Output:
# Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
#  feature/user-profile -> main

data.text: When the target branch has no new commits since the feature branch diverged, Git simply moves the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is created. This produces a perfectly linear history.

data.title: Fast-Forward Merge
data.code:
# main has not moved since feature branch started
git checkout main
git merge feature/user-profile

# main now points to the same commit as feature/user-profile

data.title: Disable Fast-Forward When You Want History
data.text: Use git merge --no-ff to force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. This preserves the record that a feature branch existed.

Rebasing transplants a branch onto a new base. Git takes the commits from your branch and replays them on top of the target branch, as if you had started your work from the latest tip. The result is a linear history with no merge commits.

data.title: Rebase Example
data.code:
git checkout feature/user-profile
git rebase main

# feature/user-profile is now based on the latest main

data.title: History Comparison
data.code:
# Before merge
a---b---c (main)
     \
      d---e (feature)

# After merge
# a---b---c---f (main)
#      \     /
#       d---e

# After rebase
# a---b---c---d'---e' (main and feature)

Produces a clean, linear history

Makes git log and git bisect easier to read

data.title: Merge for Shared Branches
data.text: On protected branches like main, use merge or squash-merge. Reserve rebase for local feature branches.

items: Cleaning up local commits before opening a pull request
Keeping a feature branch up to date with main
Teams that value a linear history and are comfortable with force pushes
Trunk-based development with short-lived branches

data.text: Squash merging is a hybrid approach. It collapses all commits from a feature branch into a single commit on the target branch. The main history stays clean, but the detailed history remains on the feature branch.

data.title: Squash Merge via CLI
data.code:
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature/user-profile

git commit -m "feat(profile): add user profile page"

data.title: Squash for Clean Main History
data.text: Use squash-merge when your team values a readable main branch but still wants full commit detail on feature branches for debugging.
When Git cannot fast-forward, it performs a three-way merge. It finds the common ancestor of both branches and combines changes from each side.

data.title: Three-Way Merge Visualization
data.code:
# Common ancestor
#       A
#      / \
#     B   C
#      \ /
#       D

# B and C diverge from A; D is the merge result

data.text: Git offers several merge strategies: ort, recursive, resolve, octopus, and ours. Each is suited to different scenarios. For most daily work, the ort strategy is recommended.

data.title: Selecting a Merge Strategy
data.code:
git merge -s ort feature/branch-a

# Or resolve for simple two-branch merges
git merge -s resolve feature/branch-b

data.text: The best merge strategy is the one your team agrees on and applies consistently. Document the convention in a CONTRIBUTING.md file and enforce it through pull request templates and branch protection rules.

items: Main branch: merge or squash-merge only
Feature branches: rebase onto main before PR
Release branches: no-ff merge to preserve release events
Hotfix branches: merge back to main and develop
Rebase is always better than merge - false, it depends on context
Merge commits are bad - false, they preserve useful branch context
Rebase is dangerous - false, it is safe on local, unpushed branches
You must rebase before every merge - false, only rebase when it improves clarity

data.text: Many teams use both merge and rebase. A common pattern is to rebase feature branches locally, then squash-merge them into main. This gives clean local history and clean main history.

data.title: Hybrid Workflow
data.code:
# Local cleanup
git rebase -i origin/main

# Push rewritten branch
git push origin --force-with-lease

# On GitHub, click "Squash and merge"

data.text: Conflicts during merge and rebase require manual resolution. The difference is that merge resolves the conflict once, while rebase may require resolving the same conflict multiple times if it touches several commits.

data.title: Rebase Conflict Storm
data.text: If a feature branch is far behind main, rebasing may trigger many conflict resolutions. In that case, a single merge may be faster and less error-prone.
The sections below go deeper into merge internals and rebase mechanics that matter in larger repositories — and in senior-level interviews.

A merge commit has two parents. The first parent is the branch you were on when you ran git merge. The second parent is the branch you merged in. This two-parent structure preserves the full branch topology.

data.title: Inspecting a Merge Commit
data.code:
git show --pretty=raw HEAD

# Output shows two parent lines:
# parent abc1234 (first parent, current branch)
# parent def5678 (second parent, merged branch)

data.text: Fast-forward is the simplest merge: Git just moves the branch pointer forward. No new commit is created. Use --no-ff when you want to preserve the record that a feature branch existed.

data.title: Fast-Forward vs No-FF
data.code:
# Fast-forward (default)
git merge feature/login

# No fast-forward
git merge --no-ff feature/login

data.text: ORT is the modern default merge strategy, introduced in Git 2.34. It handles renames better than recursive and produces cleaner merge results. Most users never need to specify it explicitly.
Recursive was the older default. It is still supported and can be useful when you need specific options such as patience or diff-algorithm tweaks. For new repositories, prefer ORT.
Merge drivers handle conflicts for specific file types. You can configure Git to always accept one side, run a custom merge tool, or use a specific strategy for certain files.

data.title: Custom Merge Driver
data.code:
[merge "ours"]
    name = Keep ours merge driver
    driver = true

[merge "package-lock"]
    name = package-lock merge driver
    driver = node merge-package-lock.js %A %O %B

data.text: Rebase compares each commit against the upstream branch using patch-id, a hash of the commit's diff (ignoring line numbers and whitespace). Commits whose patch-id already exists upstream are recognised as duplicates and dropped, which is why you never re-apply the same change twice after pulling.

data.title: Inspecting a Commit's Patch ID
data.code:
# Show the patch-id Git uses to detect duplicate commits
git show HEAD | git patch-id --stable

# Find commits that are already upstream
# (rebase drops these automatically)
git cherry --verbose origin/main

data.text: If a rebase drops all of a commit's changes because they are already present upstream, Git produces an empty commit and stops by default. Keep it with git commit --allow-empty, or tell Git how to treat empties with --empty=drop, --empty=keep, or --empty=ask (Git 2.26+).

data.title: Handling Empty Commits
data.code:
# Drop commits that became empty during the rebase
git rebase -i --empty=drop origin/main

# Or keep them without stopping
git rebase -i --empty=keep origin/main

data.text: Line ending differences between branches can cause conflicts during rebase. Configure .gitattributes to normalize line endings and reduce spurious conflicts.
CI systems typically perform a merge or rebase before running tests. Understand how your CI integrates branches to avoid surprises. Some CIs merge the PR branch with base, while others rebase.

items: GitHub Actions: merges the PR branch with base by default
GitLab CI: can be configured for merge or rebase
Bitbucket: uses merge by default
Custom CI: choose based on team convention

data.text: Enforce merge conventions with branch protection rules and required status checks. For example, require linear history on main by disallowing merge commits and mandating rebase-merge.

items: Disallow merge commits on main
Require branches to be up to date with main
Block merges if CI is failing
Require at least one approval

data.text: Customize merge commit messages to include useful context. The default message is fine for most cases, but a custom message can link to the pull request or explain why the merge was necessary.

data.title: Custom Merge Message
data.code: git merge --no-ff feature/login -m "Merge feature/login: add OAuth2 login flow (closes #234)"

data.text: When you rebase and force push, the merge request updates automatically on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. Reviewers see the new commits and can re-approve if needed.

data.title: Update PR After Rebase
data.text: After rebasing, add a comment in the PR explaining what changed. This helps reviewers understand why the diff looks different.
When squash-merging, GitHub can use the pull request title and description as the commit message. Configure this in repository settings to ensure clean, descriptive commit messages on main.

data.title: Squash Message Configuration
data.code:
# In GitHub repository settings
# Allow squash merging
# Use PR title and description as commit message

data.text: If two branches have diverged significantly, a rebase may produce many conflicts. In this case, a merge is often faster and less error-prone. Do not force a rebase just for the sake of linear history.

items: Assess the number of divergent commits
Consider the complexity of conflicts
Choose merge for large, long-lived branches
Choose rebase for short-lived, frequently updated branches

data.text: Some teams maintain their work as patch series that are regularly rebased onto main. This is common in kernel development and open-source projects where linear history is valued.

items: Maintain work as a series of patches
Rebase onto upstream regularly
Send patches to mailing list or pull request
Keep patches small and independent

data.text: Both merge and rebase are valid integration strategies. Merge preserves history and is safe on shared branches. Rebase produces linear history and moves conflicts to the developer. Choose based on team convention, branch protection rules, and the desired history shape.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Merge preserves branch history and is safe everywhere
Rebase produces linear history but requires local-only usage
Agree on a team convention and document it
